The View from SomewherePart III · Surveys that overlap

Chapter 14

The bracket

Web edition. Figure 14.5 is live: you can move the drift, change the weight and switch the misreport, and the linear programs are solved again in the page.

Here is an invented case. A four-point question, “how satisfied are you with your rent?”, with answers from 1 (very dissatisfied) to 4 (very satisfied), is asked in two different surveys of one city. Survey 1 pairs it with a question about the respondent’s car (Y) and survey 2 pairs it with a question about working from home (Z); a third survey pairs the car and home-work questions. Call the rent question X. In survey 2 it comes straight after a block of questions about utility bills, and the people who answer it are, on average, a little more satisfied than the people in survey 1. The two margins of X differ.

Chapter 13 introduced the cut rule, which keeps the analysis going when margins differ. With ordered answers one admits only the cuts, the splits “answer at most l” against “answer above l”, and a joint law of all six answers is accepted if each copy of X agrees with the other as often as its margin allows at every cut. An upward drift passes that rule, and so do a pull toward the middle and a push toward the extremes. This chapter asks what the leniency costs. If the rule forgives the drift, how much real contradiction between the three tables can the drift hide, and can we say so from the tables alone?

The answer is a bracket, and both of its ends are computed from the data. The lower end is the shortfall the cut rule reports. The upper end adds one more observable number, the area between two distribution functions. By the end of the chapter the reader will have seen why that is true, drawn three ways, and seen what happens to it when each table is a survey of a thousand people.

14.1Six copies and three numbers

Each survey measures its own copy of each variable, so there are six copies: X1,Y1 in survey 1, X2,Z2 in survey 2 and Y3,Z3 in survey 3 (Chapter 11 wrote them X1,Y1,…, with the survey as a subscript). A coupling is a joint distribution of all six that reproduces the three tables. Three quantities describe a system of tables on ordered answers.

  • C, the cut shortfall. At a cut l the best two copies a,b of one variable can do is agree with probability min{Fa(l),Fb(l)} on being at most l, where F is a distribution function. A coupling falls short of that by min{Fa(l),Fb(l)}−P(a≤l, b≤l). Add the shortfalls over the cuts and the three variables, and take the coupling that makes the total smallest. That is C. It is zero exactly when the cut rule accepts the tables. Its unit is expected scale points, so recoding the scale changes its size and never its sign.

  • D, the least total distance. Over all couplings, the smallest value of ∑V∈{X,Y,Z}E|Vi−Vj|, where Vi,Vj are the two copies of V.

  • W, the margin gap. For each variable the sum over cuts of |F1(l)−F2(l)|, added over the three variables. It depends only on the margins, so it is observable without any optimization.

Figure 14.1 shows how the six copies sit. The tables tie copies together within a survey, and D measures how far apart one must hold the copies of the same variable in order to satisfy all three tables at once.

14.2The area between two distribution functions

Take one variable and ignore the other two for a moment. Two copies a and b with distribution functions Fa and Fb. Here is an invented pair of margins on the four-point scale: Fa=(0.35, 0.65, 0.85, 1),Fb=(0.20, 0.50, 0.80, 1).Fa=(0.35, 0.65, 0.85, 1),Fb=(0.20, 0.50, 0.80, 1). Figure 14.2 draws both as step functions. The sum over cuts of |Fa(l)−Fb(l)| is the area of the three shaded rectangles, because each cut sits on a unit of horizontal width: W=0.15+0.15+0.05=0.35.

W has a second meaning, the one it earns its name from. Imagine moving probability mass along the scale to turn Fa into Fb, paying one unit of cost for each unit of mass moved one step. The cheapest way costs exactly W. This is the earth mover’s distance between the two margins, the one-dimensional case of the optimal-transport distance, and we state the standard fact here without a source read for this book. The next section proves the fact from scratch, for the case we need.

14.3What a cut can see

Now the two copies must also be coupled: a joint distribution π(a,b) with the margins above. Fix a cut l. Two regions of the (a,b) plane matter, shown in Figure 14.3: R1={a≤l<b},R2={b≤l<a}.R1={a≤l<b},R2={b≤l<a}. They are the two ways of crossing the cut: a is on the low side and b on the high side, or the other way round. The agreement we want to be large is P(a≤l, b≤l), and Fa(l)=P(a≤l,b≤l)+P(R1),Fb(l)=P(a≤l,b≤l)+P(R2).Fa(l)=P(a≤l,b≤l)+P(R1),Fb(l)=P(a≤l,b≤l)+P(R2). Subtract. Whatever the coupling, (14.1)P(R1)−P(R2)=Fa(l)−Fb(l). The coupling cannot choose the difference between the two crossing probabilities, because the margins have already chosen it. It can choose how large they both are. Their sum is therefore P(R1)+P(R2)=|Fa(l)−Fb(l)|+2min{P(R1),P(R2)}. The part |Fa(l)−Fb(l)| is unavoidable and the part 2min is waste: probability that crosses the cut in both directions at once.

Two observations turn this into a statement about distance. First, a distance of j scale steps between a and b crosses exactly j cuts, so E|a−b|=∑l[P(R1l)+P(R2l)]=Wab+2∑lmin{P(R1l),P(R2l)}. Second, the waste at cut l is the shortfall. If Fa(l)≤Fb(l) then P(R1)≤P(R2) by (14.1), and min{Fa,Fb}−P(a≤l,b≤l)=Fa−(Fa−P(R1))=P(R1), the smaller crossing probability. When Fa(l)≥Fb(l) the roles swap. So for one coupling of one variable, (14.2)E|a−b|=Wab+2(shortfall of that coupling).

Look at what the cut rule asks. It asks for a coupling with no waste: mass may cross each cut, but only toward the side the margins require. That is the picture in Kujala and Dzhafarov’s Theorem 17 (below), and it is what Figure 14.4 draws for the margins of this section. The left panel is the quantile coupling, which sorts both copies by rank and pairs them. It puts no mass in R2 at any cut, has E|a−b|=0.35=W, and shows that the cheapest transport costs W. The right panel mixes it half and half with independence. The margins are the same, the difference of crossing masses at every cut is the same, and E|a−b| is 0.775: that is 0.35 plus twice a waste of 0.2125, summed over the three cuts. The arithmetic reproduces (14.2) to 10−16.

14.4The identity

Now put the three variables back. Add (14.2) over the three variables. For any coupling of the six copies, ∑VE|Vi−Vj|=W+2(total shortfall of that coupling). W is the same for every coupling, because it depends only on the margins. Minimize the left side over all couplings and you get D; minimize the total shortfall over the same set of couplings and you get C; the two minimizers coincide. Therefore (14.3)D=W+2C for any three tables on an ordered scale. The least possible total distance between copies is a part W that the margins force and a part 2C that the contradiction among the tables forces. With equal margins, W=0 and C=D/2.

This is an algebraic identity, not a conjecture, but it is worth running because the arithmetic that was done by hand can be wrong in a hundred places. Research cycle 12 solved both linear programs on random systems and compared. The identity held to 6×10−15 in the worst of 360 misreported four-value systems (60 base systems, six misreports each). Our own implementation, written for this chapter, reproduced it to about 5×10−15 on the 34 points of Figure 14.5. The review of cycle 17 confirmed the identity again, independently.

14.5The bracket

Suppose the true tables have equal margins, so W0=0 and D0=2C0 by (14.3). C0 is the incoherence we wish we could see. Now survey 2 misreports X: it records, in place of the true answer, a value that differs by some random amount, and the expected distance between the true and the recorded answer is m. What we observe is the reported system, with shortfall C and margin gap W. How far can C be from C0?

Two steps. First, the triangle inequality. Take an optimal coupling of the true system and attach to it the recorded answer, drawn as a random function of the true answer and of Z; this is a coupling of the reported system that costs at most m more. In the other direction, attach the true answer to a coupling of the reported system through its conditional law given the recorded answer and Z. So |D−D0|≤m. Second, substitute (14.3) on both sides: C0−12(m+W)≤C≤C0+12(m−W). Nothing has been assumed about the misreport, except that the other five copies are reported truly.

Now bring in the assumption the cut rule makes. A misreport the cut rule admits crosses every cut in one direction only: upward drift, a pull toward the middle and a push toward the extremes all qualify. For such a misreport, the probability that the recorded answer lies across cut l from the true one is exactly |F1(l)−F2(l)| by (14.1), since the other crossing probability is zero. Sum over the cuts: the expected distance moved, m, equals the margin gap, W. Put m=W in the two inequalities: (14.4)C≤C0≤C+W An admitted misreport never raises the shortfall, which is why in cycle 10 the cut rule raised no false alarm of any size from such misreports. And the true incoherence is at least the observed shortfall and at most the observed shortfall plus the observed gap between the margins. Report all three numbers, C, W and C+W: the first is the part of the contradiction the cut rule can see, the second is how much the shared margins moved, and together they say how much could be hiding.

Figure 14.5 makes this concrete on the structured design of cycles 10, 11, 13 and 14. Four values, uniform margins, tables (X,Y) and (X,Z) put weight w on the diagonal and table (Y,Z) weight w on the reverse diagonal, the rest uniform. This design is invented by the research, not drawn from data. The three tables glue exactly when w≤13, and for larger w the true shortfall is C0>0. Survey 2 then misreports X by moving a share s of respondents up one step, and Figure 14.5 traces C, C+W and C0 as s grows.

Three things to see in the figure. The truth stays inside the band at every one of the 34 points plotted, as it must. The band widens linearly, because W=0.75s in this design: each of the three cuts has the distribution function drop by s/4. And the lower end is not the truth. At w=0.5 and s=0.4 the shortfall falls from 0.1875 to 0.069, a loss of 0.119 against a margin gap W=0.30. In this design the drift hid a good part of the contradiction but not all that the gap could pay for. On the right, with C0=0.05 and W already 0.225 at s=0.3, it hid everything.

Where the bracket stops being true

The bracket needs a misreport that crosses each cut one way and a single misreported copy of each variable, and both can fail. These checks are ours, computed for this chapter with the same code as Figure 14.5 at w=0.5, where C0=0.1875.

A misreport that moves answers both ways. Symmetric noise, one step up or one step down with probability s/2 each, leaves a uniform margin exactly where it was, so W=0, while the expected distance moved is m=0.15 at s=0.2 and 0.30 at s=0.4 scale steps. The reported shortfall is 0.175 and 0.1625. The general inequality still holds, as it must; but (14.4) would claim C0=C, which is false. The tables show no gap and the truth is different.

A two-way misreport that follows the other answer. Moving X one step toward Z with probability s also crosses cuts in both directions; following Z is not itself the trouble, since a one-way drift that depends on Z is still admitted. Here the shortfall rises, to 0.2125 at s=0.2 and 0.2375 at s=0.4, above the truth, with W only 0.025 and 0.05. The left inequality of (14.4) fails.

Both copies drifting alike. If both surveys that ask X push answers up by the same s, the two margins still agree, W=0, and the bracket claims C0=C. At s=0.2 the shortfall is 0.1406 and at s=0.4 it is 0.1094.

Cycle 12 checked the general form of the inequality, with the measured m, on the two non-admitted mechanisms and it held, as the algebra says. What fails is the use of W in place of m. The data cannot supply m.

14.6What the papers say

What the paper says: Kujala, Dzhafarov and Larsson (2015)

We read the main text in full. Each measurement in each context is its own random variable; if the copies of one property have different distributions no joint law can make them equal. The authors ask instead for a joint law in which copies agree as often as their margins allow, set the margin differences aside as a separate and trivial kind of context dependence (the group’s later papers call them direct influences), and ask whether the rest can be glued. For a cycle of n two-valued properties they give a necessary and sufficient condition in which the margin differences enter as an allowance, and for n=3 with uniform margins we checked numerically that it is the triangle inequality of Chapter 8. Our reading, which we have not worked through beyond that case, is that for two-valued variables the bracket (14.4) is what that condition says. The paper does not treat ordered answers with more than two values, and its inference is a conservative Bonferroni interval.

What the paper says: Dzhafarov, Cervantes and Kujala (2017), “Contextuality in canonical systems of random variables”

Sections 1 to 5 read in full, the supplement not. For many-valued variables they represent each measurement through two-way splits and ask for maximal agreement on each; an obstacle appears, a failure of what they call nominal dominance, that tells you the system is contextual from the margins alone. For ordered values they suggest it may be natural to allow only runs of successive values, name cuts as a stronger restriction, and leave the theory to later work.

What the paper says: Kujala and Dzhafarov (2022), “Contextuality and dichotomizations of random variables”

Sections 1 and 4 to 8 read, Sections 2 and 3 (formal definitions) not. This is the later work. For ordered values the admitted splits are the cuts. Their Theorem 16 says that with cuts a single connection, one variable measured in several contexts, is never contextual by itself, because the quantile coupling is admitted. Their Theorem 17 says which couplings of two copies are admitted: those whose mass avoids, at every cut, the quadrant that crosses against the sign of Fi−Fj, and both crossing quadrants where the distribution functions are equal. That is the empty region R2 of Figure 14.4. In the sections we read there is no transport distance and no statement of how much a margin gap can hide. In their framework the ordering of the values is an input supplied by the analyst, and treating the same five-point scale as ordered or as five labels can change the verdict.

What the paper says: Kujala and Dzhafarov (2019); Dzhafarov, Kujala and Cervantes (2020)

These turned up in a search for measures of contextuality. Of the first we read the abstract and one passage of the conclusion; the second we did not read. The search, one web query and one query of the stored texts, found measures built as L1 distances to a polytope for two-valued systems and nothing stated with a transport distance. Combined with the partial reading above, that is why the bracket is listed as probably known and not found stated. Both steps of the proof are elementary and we should expect someone has them.

What the paper says: Kitamura and Stoye (2018), “Nonparametric analysis of random utility models”; Fang and Santos (2019), “Inference on directionally differentiable functions”

These enter at the end of the chapter. Kitamura and Stoye test whether a vector lies in a cone and handle the boundary by shrinking the cone before resampling; we read their procedure and not their proof. Fang and Santos show that the ordinary bootstrap of a function that is only directionally differentiable can fail, and give a repair; we read the abstract and Sections 3.2 and 3.3, which state those two results. The shortfall C is such a function, and Chapter 15 is about what follows.

14.7What we found

Cycle 12: checking the bracket

Experiment 12 took 600 random four-value systems, diffuse and concentrated, coherent and not, and applied six misreports to each, 3,600 cases in all. Of the 600 systems, 124 had C0>0.01. The identity held to 6×10−15 on 360 of the misreported systems, and neither side of the general inequality failed in any of the 3,600 cases. In the four admitted mechanisms m=W to rounding error and the shortfall was never raised.

Misreport m=W Raised C Allowance used Median W/C0
shift-up yes 0 1.00 3.9
to-middle yes 0 0.65 2.6
to-extremes yes 0 0.67 2.5
shift-up on Z yes 0 0.70 1.9
noise no 0 n/a 0.86
assimilate no 8.7% of systems n/a 1.9

“Allowance used” is the median over the 124 systems of (C0−C)/min{W,C0}, the share of the most that could have been hidden that was hidden. Shift-up hid all of it in the median case, and the other three admitted misreports about two thirds. The margin gap was typically two to four times C0, which explains why cycle 11 found so little incoherence left after a drift. Of the incoherent systems with W≥C0, shift-up left C at zero in 61 percent, and the other three in 30, 32 and 33 percent.

Two caveats the notebook records and we repeat. A check of 3,600 cases tests algebra we already believe and is not evidence for a conjecture. The identity has since been confirmed by an independent review, but the triangle step has been read by nobody but us. And the bracket is for one misreported copy per variable, as the previous section showed. The first run of the script also crashed on an import and was fixed before any number was produced.

Cycle 13: the bracket from samples

Now each table is a sample of n respondents. Cycle 13 built an interval for C0 by the basic bootstrap: resample each table from its estimate, take the lower end L=max{0,2C^−q0.975(C∗)} and the upper end U=2B^−q0.025(B∗) with B=C+W, and declare incoherence when a one-sided 5 percent lower bound on C exceeds zero. Four values, uniform margins, the design above, shift-up drift, 200 replications and 150 resamples per cell:

Covers C0 Declares
Case C0 C W n=1000 4000 n=1000 4000
Coherent 0 0 0 100% 100% 0 0
Coherent, drift 0.4 0 0 0.30 100% 100% 0 0
Incoherent 0.19 0.19 0 99.5% 98.0% 99% 100%
Incoherent, drift 0.2 0.19 0.11 0.15 100% 100% 95% 100%
Incoherent, drift 0.4 0.19 0.07 0.30 100% 100% 54% 96.5%
Hidden, drift 0.4 0.05 0 0.30 100% 100% 0 0

C and W are population values of the reported tables. The interval covers in every cell and never declares a coherent system incoherent. A coverage of 100 percent with 200 replications means above about 98 percent, so the table cannot rank cells near the top. In the hidden cell the drift has used up all the slack at the population level: C=0, so no sample size can detect the incoherence. The interval covers it through its upper end, which is what the bracket was for.

The surprise is the direction of the bias. The estimated shortfall sits below its population value, 0.13 against 0.19 at n=1000 and 0.16 at n=4000 with no misreport at all. The identity explains it. The identity holds exactly for any tables, sampled or not, so C^=(D^−W^)/2. The estimated gap W^ is positive even when the true margins agree, because it is a sum of absolute values of noisy differences. With uniform margins and n=1000 the normal approximation to E|F^1−F^2| at a cut is 2/π times the standard deviation of the difference, which is 2F(1−F)/n, and summing over three cuts and three variables gives 0.146. A simulation of ours, 20,000 samples with seed 14001, gave 0.1465 at n=1000 and 0.0731 at n=4000; cycle 13’s own cell had 0.151 and 0.071. The upward bias in W^ is larger than the one in D^. In our replication of the incoherent cell at n=1000 (400 samples, standard error 0.0014), D^ averaged 0.404 against a true 0.375, W^ averaged 0.144 against zero, and so C^ averaged 0.130 against 0.1875. Cycle 13’s figure for that cell is 0.131. Noise in the margins acts like an admitted misreport: the cut rule treats the apparent margin gap as an excuse and spends it on the contradiction.

Two consequences. The test is conservative where margins are equal or nearly so, which is why this table has no false declarations. And the upper end is wide: 0.19 at n=1000 and 0.09 at n=4000 for a coherent system with equal margins (Figure 14.6), shrinking about as 1/n, because the upper end carries the noise in W^.

The memo’s first statement of this was too broad. It said the downward bias makes the test conservative, without qualification. That holds where the margins are equal or nearly equal. It does not hold at the hidden edge, where drift has used up the slack so that the population sits exactly on the boundary C=0: cycles 16 and 17 found C^>0 in 13 to 26 percent of samples there from n=1000 up, at drifts of 0.1 to 0.4, as against the nominal 5 and not shrinking with n. The rule “declare incoherence when C^>0”, which cycle 15 had calibrated and called useful, was withdrawn after cycle 16. Chapter 15 explains why it fails.

Cycle 14: a debiased gap

By the identity, the bracket is D^/2∓W^/2: center D^/2, half-width W^/2. Cycle 13’s width came from noise in W^, so the obvious repair is to correct each term |F^1(l)−F^2(l)| for its sampling variance. The two copies come from different surveys, so with δ^ the estimated difference and v its variance, δ^2−v is unbiased for the squared gap, and W~=∑max{0,δ^2−v}. Three intervals on cycle 13’s cells, seeds and resamples: the original (A); a debiased one (B) with lower and upper statistics (D^∓W~)/2; and a hybrid (H) that keeps A’s lower end and test and takes B’s upper end. At n=1000:

Covers C0 Declares Mean width
Case A B H A B A B H
Coherent 100 4 99.5 0 96 0.19 0.11 0.14
Coherent, drift 0.4 100 3 100 0 98 0.48 0.43 0.45
Incoherent 99.5 91.5 96.5 99 100 0.22 0.13 0.18
Incoherent, drift 0.4 100 100 100 54 88.5 0.49 0.45 0.47
Hidden, drift 0.4 100 98.5 100 0 94.5 0.48 0.43 0.45

Coverage and declarations are percentages; H declares exactly as A does. Column A reproduces cycle 13 exactly. B’s 94.5 percent in the hidden row is not power: the population shortfall there is zero, so it is the same false-alarm mechanism as in the coherent rows.

The debiased interval fails badly. B declares a coherent system incoherent in 96 to 98 percent of samples, and does so at n=4000 as at n=1000. The reason is the boundary. Where the cut rule finds no shortfall, D=W holds as an equality, so D^ carries the entire upward bias of W^; subtracting the smaller corrected W~ leaves a positive remainder that is all noise. The bias in the lower end is not a bias in W alone but in the boundary between C=0 and C>0, the same difficulty that Kitamura and Stoye’s shrunken cone addresses. We expected B to fail after a three-replication trial and designed H after seeing that trial, so H is a patch and not a prediction.

H is valid in these cells and buys a little. The interval narrows by about a quarter for a coherent system with equal margins (0.19 to 0.14 at n=1000 and 0.09 to 0.07 at n=4000), and by roughly 4 to 10 percent when a real drift is present, with coverage between 95.5 and 100 percent. It adds no power. Its worst coverage, 95.5 percent, is at n=4000 for the incoherent system with no drift; with 200 replications that is consistent with 95 percent but does not show that each end reaches the 97.5 percent it is built for, and the upper end is shown to be valid only in these cells. W~ itself still runs high where the gap is zero, 0.07 against 0.15 for W^, because the square root of the positive part of a noisy quantity cannot average to zero.

What remains, for ordered survey tables, is the interval [C^, C^+W~] with the hybrid’s upper end, and a test whose power under drift is modest at n=1000. Everything here is one design: uniform margins, one drift mechanism, four values, 200 replications per cell, a bootstrap used at a boundary where its validity is not established, and no comparison with Kitamura and Stoye’s tightening.

What the memo says now

The finding as the memo records it, after the review of cycle 17: under the ordered reading, and if misreports are of the admitted kind, true incoherence lies between the observed shortfall C and C+W, with W the transport distance between the shared margins. It is probably known and we did not find it stated. A bootstrap version covered in every simulated cell. Sampling noise in the margins biases the shortfall down when the shared margins are equal or nearly so, so the test is conservative there. A variance-corrected gap narrows the upper end by up to a quarter; the lower end and the test need a calibration that knows about the boundary.
